content.text:
The message you are seeing is the **shared studio cap**, not a per-person limit. Every phone shares one daily budget, and that budget is already used up for today (UTC).

There are two separate limits:

| What blocks you | Who it applies to | Message | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `generation_limit` | **Everyone together** | The studio has reached today's generation limit. | **4 pieces per UTC day** |
| `install_allowance` | **One phone** | This phone has made today's pieces. | 8 pieces per phone per UTC day |

Each new piece reserves 1 Gemma attempt, 60 GPU seconds, and 1 music attempt. The defaults are 4 Gemma attempts, 240 GPU seconds, and 6 music attempts, so the studio stops after **4 pieces total**. A phone's own allowance of 8 never gets a chance to matter until that shared budget is higher. There is no account: "per user" here means one anonymous install token stored on that phone.

Those numbers are read once, when the backend process starts, from:

- `MAX_GEMMA_ATTEMPTS_PER_DAY` (default 4, code will not go above **8**)
- `MAX_GEMMA_GPU_SECONDS_PER_DAY` (default 240, code will not go above **480**)
- `MAX_MUSIC_ATTEMPTS_PER_DAY` (default 6, code will not go above **8**)
- `MAX_INSTALL_JOBS_PER_DAY` (default 8, code will not go above **8**)

`deploy/render.yaml` still sets the shared caps to 4, 240, and 6. The live Render dashboard can differ from that file. Today's usage is already stored in the quota ledger, so raising the cap and restarting lets more pieces through the same day. The count resets at **00:00 UTC** (05:30 IST).

**To allow up to 8 pieces a day for the whole studio**, set these on the running service (Render environment, or `backend/.env` locally) and restart the process:

```
MAX_GEMMA_ATTEMPTS_PER_DAY=8
MAX_GEMMA_GPU_SECONDS_PER_DAY=480
MAX_MUSIC_ATTEMPTS_PER_DAY=8
```

GPU seconds must stay at least `pieces × 60`. Eight pieces need 480 seconds. Anything above 8, 480, or 8 is ignored until the hard ceilings in `backend/app/jobs/service.py` (`_GEMMA_MAX`, `_GPU_MAX`, `_MUSIC_MAX`, `_INSTALL_MAX`) are raised in code.

Raising the shared cap spends more Hugging Face Gemma and ElevenLabs quota. The project notes say that deployed cap should be confirmed against those budgets before it is changed.

Tell me the daily numbers you want (shared studio total, and per phone) and whether this is local or the Render service, and I can make the code and config match.

content.text:
The studio is stopping you on the shared daily budget, which is 4 pieces for every phone together. A per-phone allowance of 8 already exists, and it never applies until that shared budget is higher. This plan only raises those ceilings. It does not change generation behavior, error copy, or the ledger format.

## Target to confirm before any edit

Use these numbers unless you want different ones:

| Limit | Now | Planned |
|---|---|---|
| One phone per UTC day | 8, and the code refuses anything higher | **20** |
| Whole studio, Gemma attempts | 4, code ceiling 8 | **40** |
| Whole studio, GPU seconds | 240 (4 × 60) | **2400** (40 × 60) |
| Whole studio, music attempts | 6, code ceiling 8 | **40** |

Each accepted piece still reserves 1 Gemma attempt, 60 GPU seconds, and 1 music attempt. GPU seconds must stay at least `pieces × 60`, or a job is refused even when the attempt counters still have room. One active piece at a time stays as it is. Counts still reset at 00:00 UTC (05:30 IST).

At 20 per phone, two phones can each finish a full day. A third phone is stopped by the shared budget after the studio has made 40 pieces. That shared budget is what produces “The studio has reached today's generation limit.” The per-phone message stays “This phone has made today's pieces.”

These calls spend Hugging Face Gemma time and ElevenLabs music credits. Confirm that 40 arrangements and 40 tracks per UTC day is an acceptable bill before this is deployed.

## What will change

1. **Raise the hard ceilings** in `backend/app/jobs/service.py`. `bounded_cap` ignores any environment value above `_INSTALL_MAX` (8), `_GEMMA_MAX` (8), `_GPU_MAX` (480), and `_MUSIC_MAX` (8). Set those ceilings to at least 20, 40, 2400, and 40. Leave the defaults at 8, 4, 240, and 6 so an unset environment still means today’s behavior.

2. **Set the four environment variables** on the process that is actually serving you, then restart it. The caps are read once at import, so a running process keeps the old numbers until it restarts.
   - Local: `backend/.env`
   - Render: the service dashboard for https://footwork-m6g0.onrender.com/, which can differ from the committed blueprint
   ```
   MAX_INSTALL_JOBS_PER_DAY=20
   MAX_GEMMA_ATTEMPTS_PER_DAY=40
   MAX_GEMMA_GPU_SECONDS_PER_DAY=2400
   MAX_MUSIC_ATTEMPTS_PER_DAY=40
   ```

3. **Update the committed blueprint** in `deploy/render.yaml` to those same four values, and update the matching assertions in `backend/tests/unit/test_health.py`. That test currently requires the blueprint to say 4, 240, and 6. `MAX_INSTALL_JOBS_PER_DAY` is not in the blueprint today; add it there so the per-phone cap is visible next to the shared ones.

4. **Adjust quota tests** in `backend/tests/unit/test_jobs.py`. The clamp test expects 30, 100, and 99999 to be cut down to 8, 8, 480, and 8. Point those expectations at the new ceilings. The “four jobs then `generation_limit`” test should keep passing, because it uses the defaults. Add one case where the shared budget is open and the 21st job from the same install token returns `install_allowance`.

5. **Document the new ceilings** in `backend/.env.example` only. Leave the user-facing strings in `generationContract.ts` and `service.py` unchanged.

Today’s ledger is kept. After restart, new jobs are allowed only while today’s already-spent Gemma, GPU, and music counters are still under the new caps. Delete does not refund a reservation.

## Check before calling it done

- A 5th piece from the same phone is accepted after the restart, and the response is not `generation_limit`.
- The 21st piece from that phone returns `install_allowance` and does not call Gemma or Eleven.
- A second install token still has its own count of 20.
- Backend unit tests for jobs and health pass.
- No frontend change is required. The existing error screens already explain both limits.

Say if those daily numbers should be different. After that, implementation can start.

def _release_cap(name: str, default: int, maximum: int) -> int:
    """Return the env value for name, or default when unset or invalid, never above maximum."""
    raw = os.environ.get(name, "").strip()

    try:

# Architecture

Footwork turns a walk into a short instrumental and a Soundprint that shows where the movement changed the music. The locked diagram is `Docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw`. A PNG export of that diagram is not in the repository yet.

## Context

A person walks with the browser. The browser records the walk and plays the result. One Render service runs the React app and the Python API. That API asks a Hugging Face ZeroGPU Space running Gemma for an arrangement, then asks Eleven Music to render a validated plan. Gemma receives an anonymous event timeline. It does not receive coordinates or the original clock.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    U["Walker"]
    B["Browser recording and Soundprint"]
    R["Render: Python API and frontend"]
    H["Hugging Face ZeroGPU: Gemma"]
    E["Eleven Music"]
    U --> B
    B --> R
    R --> H
    R --> E
```

## What happens to one walk

1. The browser keeps the draft on the phone. Ending the walk sends it to the API over HTTPS.
2. The API cleans the trace, detects turns, pauses, pace changes, and loops, and drops coordinates before any provider call.
3. Gemma returns a constrained arrangement. An invalid plan may be repaired once, and only when daily budget and the deadline still allow it.
4. A validated plan is the only request sent to Eleven Music. The audio is checked, then stored as a protected artifact.
5. The browser plays that audio from one clock. The route, ribbon, and current moment follow that clock.
6. If arrangement or music fails, the same timeline becomes a Route Sketch on the server. The labeled example is a separate prepared piece and is not described as a live generation.

## Daily generation budget

This working tree reads three environment variables when the process starts. An empty value uses the default. A higher value is clamped to the maximum.

| Cap | Default | Maximum | Blueprint value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Gemma attempts | 4 | 40 | 40 |
| Gemma GPU seconds | 240 | 2400 | 2400 |
| Music attempts | 6 | 40 | 40 |

Each accepted piece reserves 1 Gemma attempt, 60 GPU seconds, and 1 music attempt. The budget is shared by every caller for the UTC day. This branch does not keep a separate per-phone allowance. One generation can be active at a time. Deleting a piece does not refund the reservation. `GENERATION_ENABLED` must be the string `true` before the dispatcher calls Eleven. The blueprint still lists that flag as `false` so a full blueprint sync does not turn generation on by itself.

## Trust boundaries

- Location permission and the raw draft stay in the browser until the walk is submitted.
- Provider keys stay on the server.
- The quota ledger stores hashes, not the walk, the job key, or an install token.
- A share link is a capability for about an hour. It does not contain a location and it cannot delete the piece.
- Ready audio is removed about 60 minutes after it is ready. Ledger rows stay for 48 hours.

## Sponsors

Gemma is the open-weight arranger. Render hosts the public app and API. Eleven Music renders a validated plan into audio. CodeRabbit, Entire, DevRelay, GitHub Actions, and Excalidraw are development tools. The running app does not call them.

# Demo runbook

Use this order for a 60-second demonstration. The backup video, hero screenshot, and mobile screenshot are not in the repository. Add those files before treating the demonstration as complete. Prepared playback is the labeled example. It is not a live generation.

## First ten seconds

1. Open https://footwork-m6g0.onrender.com/.
2. Show the heading "Turn a walk into music."
3. Move to "Hear what a moment does" and point at the turn, then the pause. Say that a corner is meant to change the melody's direction and a pause is meant to become a break.

## Show the prepared example

1. Choose **Hear an example**. The studio opens on "Corner and pause."
2. The page says "Example walk" and "This sound is an example made in the browser. It is not a studio recording."
3. Press **Play**. One control drives the route, the ribbon, and the current moment.
4. Seek the turn near 0:18 and the pause near 0:36. Say that these marks are planned illustrations in the example.

Do not say this press called Gemma or Eleven.

## If a live walk is available

Use a walk that has already been reviewed. Do not start a new generation during the demo unless the day's provider budget still has room. A new piece spends one Gemma attempt and, when the plan validates, one music attempt.

If generation is slow or unavailable, return to **Hear an example** and say the live studio path fell back. A Route Sketch is the simpler version made from the walk. It is not a studio recording.

## Files still to add

| Asset | Where it should go | What it must show |
|---|---|---|
| Backup video | `Docs/demo/` | The turn and pause in the first ten seconds, then the mechanism and the example label |
| Hero screenshot | `Docs/demo/` | The example at the turn marker |
| Mobile screenshot | `Docs/demo/` | The recording or result experience on a phone |
| Architecture PNG | `Docs/diagrams/` | Export of `Docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw` |

`Docs/demo/` is not created until those files exist.

## What not to claim

- The example was generated during the presentation.
- A planned musical change has been heard in a studio file, unless the heard-time sheet in `Docs/evidence/seed-walk-review.md` is filled.
- The route on screen is a map. It is an abstracted shape and contains no coordinates.

# Submission checklist

Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1. The explanation stays unpublished until it is reviewed. Do not publish from this file.

## Links

- Public app: https://footwork-m6g0.onrender.com/
- Repository: https://github.com/kernelKain/footwork
- Architecture: `Docs/architecture.md`
- Diagram source: `Docs/diagrams/architecture.excalidraw`

`#devchallenge` and `#hf26challenge`. The DEV draft also needs a clear statement that an agent helped write it.

# A walk writes the instrumental, then the Soundprint shows where

This draft is unpublished. Review it before it is posted. The backup video, screenshots, and architecture PNG are still to be added.

## The problem

A walk has a shape: a corner, a stop, a faster stretch. Most recordings of that walk throw the shape away and keep a track that could have been any song. Footwork keeps the shape and turns it into a short instrumental, then shows the same moments on the piece while it plays.

## The hook

Open the public app at https://footwork-m6g0.onrender.com/ and choose **Hear an example**. The piece is labeled Example walk. A turn sits near 0:18 and is meant to change the melody's direction. A pause sits near 0:36 and is meant to hold the sound. That example is prepared in the browser. It is not a live call to Gemma or Eleven Music.

## How movement becomes music

The phone keeps the walk locally. Ending it sends the trace to the API. The server cleans the trace and looks for a sharp turn, a pause, a pace change, and a return to an earlier part of the route. Coordinates and the original clock are removed before any model sees the walk. Gemma, `google/gemma-4-E2B-it` on a Hugging Face ZeroGPU Space, proposes a constrained instrumental arrangement from that anonymous timeline. A plan that validates is the only request sent to Eleven Music. The browser then plays one audio element, and the route, ribbon, and current moment follow that clock.

If the arrangement or the recording fails, the same timeline becomes a simpler Route Sketch on the server. The page says so.

## Why Gemma is central

Gemma is the musical director, not a caption model. It chooses the arrangement from the movement events. Render hosts the app and the API. Eleven Music renders the accepted plan. The development tools, including the agent that helped draft this explanation, are not part of that runtime.

## What was hard

The providers must not see the place. The quota has to stop a new piece before a paid call when the day's budget is gone. A lost music response must not be retried, because the request may already have been charged. The example, the Route Sketch, and a studio recording use different sentences so a listener can tell them apart.

## Limitations

The outdoor walk was reviewed, and the heard-time sheet for that studio file is not filled yet. Gemma latency for the checked plan was not measured. Eleven balance was not readable with the key in use. The demonstration video and screenshots are not attached to this draft.

## Links

- App: https://footwork-m6g0.onrender.com/
- Repository: https://github.com/kernelKain/footwork
- Architecture notes live in the repository at `Docs/architecture.md`

## Architecture

The browser records and plays. Render serves the app and the Python API. Gemma on Hugging Face ZeroGPU arranges an anonymous timeline. Eleven Music renders a validated plan. ## Local setup

Use Node 22.12 or newer and Python 3.12.12.

```bash
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run dev --prefix frontend
uv sync --directory backend
backend/.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --app-dir backend --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

Copy `backend/.env.example` to `backend/.env` and fill the provider values locally. Do not commit that file. `GENERATION_ENABLED` must be `true` before a local process calls Eleven. The daily cap variables are read from the process environment when the API starts.

## Tests and evidence

```bash
uv run --directory backend pytest
uv run --directory backend ruff check .
npm run typecheck --prefix frontend
npm run lint --prefix frontend
npm test --prefix frontend
```

Provider proofs are in `Docs/evidence/`. The listening sheet for the outdoor studio file is still empty.

## Privacy and retention

The raw walk stays on the phone until it is submitted. Providers receive event summaries, not coordinates. The ledger stores hashes. A result link lasts about an hour, does not contain a location, and cannot delete the piece. Ready audio is removed about 60 minutes after it is ready. Ledger rows stay for 48 hours. Spent quota is not refunded when a piece is deleted.

## AI-assisted development

Cursor agents helped implement and document this repository. Gemma is the in-product arranger. The explanation draft in `Docs/write-ups/footwork-challenge-draft.md` was drafted with agent assistance and is unpublished. The running app does not call the writing tools.

Application code is MIT, copyright Kshitij Jain, in `LICENSE`. The Gemma checkpoint `google/gemma-4-E2B-it` is Apache-2.0. arguments.title: A walk writes the instrumental, then the Soundprint shows where
arguments.description: Footwork turns a walk's corners and pauses into a short instrumental, and the Soundprint shows those moments while it plays.
arguments.body_markdown:
This draft is unpublished. The backup video, screenshots, and architecture PNG are still to be added.

## The problem

A walk has a shape: a corner, a stop, a faster stretch. Most recordings of that walk throw the shape away and keep a track that could have been any song. Footwork keeps the shape and turns it into a short instrumental, then shows the same moments on the piece while it plays.

## The hook

Open the public app at https://footwork-m6g0.onrender.com/ and choose **Hear an example**. The piece is labeled Example walk. A turn sits near 0:18 and is meant to change the melody's direction. A pause sits near 0:36 and is meant to hold the sound. That example is prepared in the browser. It is not a live call to Gemma or Eleven Music.

## How movement becomes music

The phone keeps the walk locally. Ending it sends the trace to the API. The server cleans the trace and looks for a sharp turn, a pause, a pace change, and a return to an earlier part of the route. Coordinates and the original clock are removed before any model sees the walk. Gemma, `google/gemma-4-E2B-it` on a Hugging Face ZeroGPU Space, proposes a constrained instrumental arrangement from that anonymous timeline. A plan that validates is the only request sent to Eleven Music. The browser then plays one audio element, and the route, ribbon, and current moment follow that clock.

If the arrangement or the recording fails, the same timeline becomes a simpler Route Sketch on the server. The page says so.

## Why Gemma is central

Gemma is the musical director, not a caption model. It chooses the arrangement from the movement events. Render hosts the app and the API. Eleven Music renders the accepted plan. The development tools, including the agent that helped draft this explanation, are not part of that runtime.

## What was hard

The providers must not see the place. The quota has to stop a new piece before a paid call when the day's budget is gone. A lost music response must not be retried, because the request may already have been charged. The example, the Route Sketch, and a studio recording use different sentences so a listener can tell them apart.

## Limitations

The outdoor walk was reviewed, and the heard-time sheet for that studio file is not filled yet. Gemma latency for the checked plan was not measured. Eleven balance was not readable with the key in use. The demonstration video and screenshots are not attached to this draft.

## Links

- App: https://footwork-m6g0.onrender.com/
- Repository: https://github.com/kernelKain/footwork
- Architecture notes live in the repository at `Docs/architecture.md`
